questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Abstraction as a decision about subject
questions.learningObjective: Explain how abstraction is a decision about what counts as the subject
questions.stem: Your field survey protocol must state why a plate of drawings of the same dune shows almost no recognisable detail, and the draft calls the work decorative.

options.text: The artist chose which features to leave out, so the subject is a decision rather than a copy.
The artist lacked the skill to depict the dune faithfully, so the result is a failure of technique.
options.misconception: reads deliberate simplification as a lack of skill

options.text: The artist was copying a scientific chart, so the subject is data rather than a decision.
options.misconception: assumes the work's subject is borrowed from a chart

options.text: The artist was paid to decorate a visitor centre, so the subject is the building's function.
options.misconception: infers a decorative commission from the subject matter

questions.explanation: Abstraction begins with a choice about what counts as the subject, so the dune can be present without its details. Lack of skill, chart-copying and decoration are causes the work does not support.
questions.hint: Ask what the artist decided to leave out.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What colour field scale does to looking
questions.learningObjective: Interpret identical data read differently because of surrounding colour
questions.stem: Coding habitat patches in your survey, you notice that two plots with identical plant counts read very differently in the field, one green-grey and one a saturated blue-green. What does the comparison suggest about large colour areas?

options.text: The plot with the blue-green field contains different species, since plant colour records species.
options.misconception: reads colour as a direct indicator of species

options.text: A large field of colour affects how the eye reads everything around it, so scale is part of the seeing.
The saturated field is simply better exposed, so the difference is a photographic fault.
options.misconception: attributes a perceptual effect to a technical error

options.text: Colour areas only matter indoors, since daylight washes out any large field of colour.
options.misconception: assumes scale of colour matters only under gallery light

questions.explanation: Identical plant counts read differently because the surrounding field of colour alters perception of the whole picture. Scale and adjacency change looking itself, not content or exposure.
questions.hint: Ask what the field of colour does to the eye.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What makes a performance a work
questions.learningObjective: Explain what turns a live action into a work
questions.stem: Writing the survey methods section, you must explain what makes a live action in a clearing count as a work rather than an event.

answer.exemplar: A performance becomes a work through the elements an event lacks: a declared duration, a prepared structure or score, an audience gathered to witness it, and a set of decisions about repetition and recording. The work is the event happening under those conditions, not the ordinary activity of the clearing. Documentation is a separate object made afterwards, and it can stand in for the work without being the work itself.

questions.explanation: A performance becomes a work through declared duration, structure, audience and intention, not through the bare occurrence of an action. Documentation made afterwards is a separate object that can stand in for the work.
questions.hint: Ask what makes the action a bounded occurrence.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total time needed for a specified multi-step procedure
questions.stem: A transect log records each station as eight minutes of work, and your protocol sets eighteen stations for the morning route. How many minutes does the route take?

questions.hint: Multiply the number of steps by the time each takes.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why an installation depends on its site
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an installation cannot be detached from its location

stimulus.body: A set of vitrines was installed in a corridor beside the field entrance, each holding specimens from the marsh within a kilometre of that building. The curator notes that the display was re-hung in a different building in 2004 and the arrangement was adjusted to fit each corridor's dimensions.

questions.stem: During your survey you encounter a specimen display in a corridor beside the field entrance, and you must explain why it belongs where it is.

options.text: Its meaning depends on the light, since the corridor's windows were chosen for the collection.
options.misconception: reduces site dependence to lighting conditions

options.text: Its meaning is carried entirely by the labels, so the building is only a convenient shelter.
options.misconception: treats meaning as carried by text alone

options.text: Its meaning depends on the relationship between the objects and this particular place, so moving it changes the work.
Its meaning is fixed by the curator's arrangement, so the specific corridor is incidental.
options.misconception: believes arrangement alone fixes what the work means

questions.explanation: An installation is completed by its relation to a particular place, so re-hanging it elsewhere alters the work rather than moving it. Labels, light and arrangement matter, but none makes the site incidental.
questions.hint: Ask what the building contributes to the work.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The readymade and the question of authorship
questions.learningObjective: Separate the act of choosing an object from the act of making it
questions.stem: Two site managers argue about whether a curator who selects an ordinary stone from a riverbank for display is the author of the resulting work.

options.text: The authorship lies in the display case, since the case determines how the object is seen.
options.misconception: treats the display furniture as the source of authorship

options.text: The authorship lies in nothing at all, because a found object cannot be made into art by selection.
options.misconception: denies that selection can constitute an artistic act

options.text: The authorship lies in the stone's natural form, so the maker of the object remains the true author.
options.misconception: attributes authorship to nature rather than to choice

options.text: The authorship lies in choosing and naming a found object, since making the object was not the act.

questions.explanation: With a found object the artistic act becomes selection and placement, so authorship moves without any making. Neither nature nor the case is the author; the case supports without creating the work.
questions.hint: Ask where the artistic act took place.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What collage does to drawing and making
questions.learningObjective: Identify the operation that makes collage a way of working
questions.stem: Your survey notes describe a display board where printed labels, map fragments and hand-drawn sketches are cut and fitted together in one field.

options.text: Collage is a display practice used to tidy a collection, so the fragments have no shared subject.
options.misconception: treats collage as an arrangement of unrelated things

options.text: Collage makes by cutting and placing, so the making method links drawing to arrangement.
Collage is a copying technique, since each fragment is taken from an existing drawing.
options.misconception: reduces collage to copying without alteration

options.text: Collage is a conservation method, since joining fragments prevents damage to the papers.
options.misconception: confuses a making method with a preservation technique

questions.explanation: Collage makes by cutting, placing and joining fragments from different sources, so drawing and arrangement become one operation. Tidying, copying and conservation do not describe what the fragments do.
questions.hint: Ask what the maker physically did to the sources.

questions.topic: Abstraction as a decision about subject
questions.learningObjective: Interpret two abstractions of one dataset
questions.stem: Comparing two seasons of survey data, your abstract diagrams of the same wetland look different although the recorded species list is identical. What does the comparison show?

options.text: The diagrams belong to different periods, so they cannot be compared with each other.
options.misconception: dismisses comparison because the images look unlike

options.text: The diagrams are inaccurate, since identical data must produce identical pictures.
options.misconception: assumes one dataset can yield only one correct picture

options.text: Abstraction is a decision about the subject, so the same data can be organised into different subjects.
Abstract diagrams are unreliable, so field records should always replace them.
options.misconception: generalises from two diagrams to a ban on drawing

questions.explanation: The same species list drawn as different diagrams shows that abstraction organises data into a chosen subject rather than copying it. Different appearances are expected, not evidence of error.
questions.hint: Compare the data, then compare the pictures.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What colour field scale does to looking
questions.learningObjective: Describe how a large colour area redirects the viewer's attention
questions.stem: Drafting the discussion section of your survey report, you must explain what happens to looking when colour covers a very large area.

answer.exemplar: A large field of colour shifts the viewer's attention away from local detail and towards relations between areas, edges and the body of the person looking. Because the field is uniform over a wide area, the eye has little to measure it against, so the surrounding colours and the dimensions of the room become conspicuous. Colour therefore becomes the material of the picture rather than a description of things, and scale is part of how the picture is made.

questions.explanation: Large colour fields redirect attention to edges, relations and the viewer's position, so colour becomes subject rather than description. The effect depends on area, making scale a formal decision.
questions.hint: Ask where the eye goes in a uniform field.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A work that is a set of instructions
questions.learningObjective: Determine the status of an instruction sheet within the work

stimulus.body: A folded card carries twelve numbered actions, each with a duration and a condition, and states that any number of people may perform it in any order. The card is the only score available, and the resulting action is recorded only in the performers' notebooks.

questions.stem: Photographing a specimen tray for the archive, you find a folded card listing twelve numbered actions and asking that any number of people perform it in any order.

options.text: The card is a score for a fixed result, since the actions leave no room for interpretation.
options.misconception: confuses specified conditions with a fully determined outcome

options.text: The card is a set of instructions for an event that exists only while it is being performed.
options.misconception: denies the instructions any status as the work itself

options.text: The card is a document about past performances, since it records what the performers did.
options.misconception: treats an instruction sheet as a record of past events

options.text: The card is the work, since it fixes the work's conditions while leaving the realisation open.

questions.explanation: An instruction-based work consists of the specified conditions, so the sheet is the work and each performance realises it. It is not a prompt, a record of the past, or a formula that fixes the result.
questions.hint: Ask which document the performances depend on.

options.misconception: reduces the site to an insurance question

options.text: The site matters only for access, since remote locations reach fewer visitors.
options.misconception: reduces the site to an audience-size question

questions.explanation: A site's meaning is completed by where a work stands, so a display linked to that landscape differs from the same playback elsewhere. Content, insurance and visitor counts are not what the site adds.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how designating an existing object can be a making
questions.stem: The survey handbook asks you to explain why an ordinary survey marker, manufactured for practical use, may be exhibited as a work.

options.misconception: claims all manufactured objects are artworks already

options.text: Because the marker's function on the landscape gives it an aesthetic quality it lacked.
options.misconception: thinks utility objects gain art status through their function

options.text: Because the act of choosing and designating an existing object can itself be the making of a work.
Because the exhibition gives the marker a new purpose, which is what makes it art.
options.misconception: reduces the work to the exhibition context alone

questions.explanation: A readymade work rests on choosing and designating an existing object, so the artistic act lies in designation rather than fabrication. Function, universal art status and context alone do not account for it.
questions.hint: Ask where the artistic act happened.

questions.stem: Reviewing your collage panel record, you find the field cut into 40 pieces, 26 of them printed map fragments and 14 of them hand-drawn sketches, and 30 pieces carry visible cut edges. What does this record support?

options.misconception: reads one majority as the rule for the method

options.text: Collage is a drawing technique, since the hand-drawn pieces give the panel its character.
options.misconception: reduces collage to the drawn fragments alone

options.text: Collage joins sources of different kinds, and cutting is the operation that lets them sit together.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Abstraction as a decision about subject
questions.learningObjective: Set out the decision that abstraction involves
questions.stem: Explaining to a volunteer what abstraction does to a subject, you must set out the decision it involves.

answer.exemplar: Abstraction is a decision about what a subject is. The maker selects certain features and relations, discards the rest, and presents the selection so that it can be seen as a subject in its own right rather than as a copy of a place or thing. What disappears is not the world but the obligation to reproduce it, and what appears is a chosen set of relations that the viewer has to read.

questions.explanation: Abstraction is a choice about what will count as the subject, not an inability to depict. Selecting some features and dropping others turns a record of the world into a subject in its own right.
questions.hint: Ask what the maker decided to keep.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What makes a performance a work
questions.learningObjective: Explain a repeated performance as one work realised again

stimulus.body: For one hour each evening a performer walks the length of a boardwalk at a fixed pace, carrying a lamp that is switched on and off at irregular intervals. The schedule is posted publicly, and a different person performs on each of the nine evenings.

options.text: The work is the ninth performance only, since earlier nights were rehearsals of the same action.
options.misconception: mistakes repeated performances for rehearsal

options.text: The work is the scheduled action itself, so each night realises it again rather than repeating one event.
The work is the lamp, since only the object changes hands between performers and objects endure.
options.misconception: reduces the work to the object used in it

options.text: The work is the poster announcing the schedule, since the announcement is what the public received.
options.misconception: substitutes the announcement for the action

questions.explanation: A repeated performance is the work realised again, so no single night is the whole of it and none is a rehearsal. The lamp and the poster are components and evidence, not the work.
questions.hint: Ask what the nine evenings share.

questions.topic: A work that is a set of instructions
questions.learningObjective: Separate what a score fixes from what it leaves open
questions.stem: In a written audit of your methods, you must separate what an instruction sheet fixes from what it leaves to performers.

options.text: It fixes nothing at all, since an instruction sheet is only a suggestion offered to performers.
options.misconception: reduces a score to mere suggestion

options.text: It fixes the entire outcome, since any performance that differs has departed from the work.
options.misconception: assumes a score determines every detail of performance

options.text: It fixes conditions and limits, while leaving the realisation open, which is where variation enters.
It fixes only the timing, since the actions themselves can be improvised freely.
options.misconception: narrows what a score specifies to timing alone

questions.explanation: An instruction sheet specifies conditions and limits while leaving the realisation open, and that gap is where performances differ. A fully determined outcome or a mere suggestion both miss the structure.
questions.hint: Ask what performers still have to decide.

options.misconception: attributes a siting rule to grant conditions

questions.explanation: Requiring a work to stay on site expresses the idea that an installation's meaning depends on where it stands. Safety, transport and funding explain practical limits, not artistic dependence.
questions.hint: Ask what the rule is really asserting.

options.misconception: assumes authorship requires fabrication rather than choice

options.text: The artistic act can lie in choosing which existing object to present, not only in making it.

options.misconception: attributes authority to age rather than to the making

questions.explanation: Two sets of six, one made and one manufactured, show that choosing an object can carry the artistic act without fabrication. Fabrication, quantity and age describe the objects but do not locate authorship.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What collage does to drawing and making
questions.learningObjective: Explain how collage changes the work of drawing
questions.stem: Writing a note for the collection register, you must explain what collage does to the idea of drawing.

answer.exemplar: Collage relocates the work of drawing into selection and arrangement. Rather than building a form mark by mark, the maker works with fragments already made by others, cuts them to shape, and composes them so that edges, overlaps and gaps create relationships that were never in the originals. Drawing's tools and skills can still be present, but the governing operation is the cut and the placement, and the result is a form that no single hand executed.

questions.explanation: Collage shifts making from mark-making to cutting and composing fragments, so drawing becomes one source among several. That is a change in the governing operation, not in the fragments' appearance.
questions.hint: Ask which operation governs the whole.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The readymade and the question of authorship
questions.learningObjective: Explain how authorship operates when nothing is made
questions.stem: Describing the rules given to a group of assistants who arrange found objects, you must explain how authorship operates when nothing is made.

answer.exemplar: When nothing is made, authorship moves to the decisions that surround an existing object: which thing is chosen out of thousands, what it is called, where it is put, and what the arrangement is meant to direct attention to. Assistants who carry out those decisions are not the author, nor is the person who first made the object in its original use. The work is the act of designation and framing applied to something already there.

questions.explanation: With found objects the artistic act is designation and placement rather than fabrication, so authorship sits with those decisions, not with the original maker. Assistants carrying them out are executors, not authors.
questions.hint: Ask which decisions count as the artistic ones.

questions.topic: Abstraction as a decision about subject
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a deliberate abstraction from an incomplete record

stimulus.body: Two plates depict the same salt-marsh profile. The first shows every measured feature at the same scale across the full width. The second keeps only the tidal height and the width of the pans, drawn as two plain bands, and every other measured feature is absent.

questions.stem: The habitat survey records the height of the marsh and the width of its pans, but omits every other measurement from the second plate.

options.text: The second plate is a copy, since the two bands reproduce measured values exactly.
options.misconception: confuses exact values with a faithful reproduction

options.text: The second plate is an abstraction because the maker was unable to draw the remaining features.
options.misconception: reads deliberate selection as a drawing failure

options.text: The second plate is a diagram, so it cannot be compared with the first plate at all.
options.misconception: treats a diagram as unrelated to the fuller plate

options.text: The second plate is an abstraction because the maker chose which relations would count as the subject.

questions.explanation: Keeping two measured relations and dropping the rest shows abstraction as a decision about the subject, not a drawing failure. Exact values make the plate a record, not a copy.
questions.hint: Ask what the second plate chooses to show.

questions.topic: What colour field scale does to looking
questions.learningObjective: Separate the effect of a colour area's extent from its intensity
questions.stem: Before you submit your methods appendix, you must separate the effect of a large colour area from the effect of its brightness.

options.text: Area and brightness are the same variable, since a larger field is always a brighter one.
options.misconception: conflates two independent properties of a colour area

options.text: Area changes how the eye reads the whole picture; brightness sets how strongly the colour asserts itself.
Only brightness matters, since the eye judges colour by intensity and ignores extent.
options.misconception: believes extent has no effect on perception

options.text: Only area matters, since the value of a colour is meaningless without its extent.
options.misconception: believes intensity cannot be judged without an area

questions.explanation: A colour field works through two separable properties: how much of the picture it occupies and how intense its value is. Treating them as one, or denying either, leaves the effect undescribed.
questions.hint: Ask how many independent variables are at work.

questions.topic: What makes a performance a work
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a performed work from an ordinary event
questions.stem: A field note describes an action carried out at dusk in front of a small audience, and you must explain what makes it a work rather than an ordinary event.

options.text: It is a work because it was performed outdoors, since location is the only thing that counts.
options.misconception: assigns artistic status to location alone

options.text: It is a work because it happened in front of people, since audiences make every event art.
options.misconception: confuses any witnessed event with a work

options.text: It is bounded, prepared and witnessed, so it exists as a work rather than as ordinary life.
It is a work only if it is recorded, since documentation is what creates the object.
options.misconception: makes documentation the source of the work's existence

questions.explanation: A performance becomes a work by being bounded, prepared and witnessed in a way that distinguishes it from ordinary events. An audience, a location and documentation can accompany one but do not make it.
questions.hint: Ask what separates it from ordinary life.

options.misconception: mistakes a difference in detail for a difference in identity

options.text: A fuller instruction set produces better performances, since detail always improves the outcome.
options.misconception: confuses more specification with better results

options.text: The shorter list is more open, and therefore more clearly a work in its own right.
options.misconception: assumes less specification makes a work truer

options.text: A fuller instruction set fixes more of the conditions under which the work is realised.

questions.explanation: Adding durations and conditions to the same twelve steps fixes more of the circumstances of realisation without changing the steps. It is not a judgement about quality, nor does it make two works.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why an installation depends on its site
questions.learningObjective: Describe what a site contributes to an installation
questions.stem: Explaining to a school group why an installation cannot simply be moved, you must describe what the site contributes.

answer.exemplar: An installation depends on a site because the site is one of the materials from which the work is made. The room's dimensions, its light, its sounds, its floor and the route visitors take through it all enter the work's structure, so that removing the work to another building does not transport the same thing but produces a different one. What can be rebuilt exactly is only the measurable part, and the meaning that depends on the place is lost with it.

questions.explanation: The site supplies material conditions of the work, so relocating an installation produces a different work rather than a copy. Replication can restore measurements but not the relation to the ground.
questions.hint: Ask what the place contributes that measurement cannot.

options.text: The panel is a montage of documents, since the fragments were produced for completely different purposes.
options.misconception: treats mixed sources as the whole meaning of the work

options.text: The cut edges and the interrupted line make relationships that exist only in the assembled panel.
The panel is a record of the original wall, since the photograph documents the whole surface.
options.misconception: reduces the collage to the photograph it contains

options.text: The panel is a design exercise, since its purpose is to show a tidy arrangement of mixed media.
options.misconception: reads the assembly as tidiness rather than argument

questions.explanation: The interrupted handwriting and overlapping cut edges create a relation that existed in none of the fragments, which is what collage produces. Mixed purposes and neatness do not account for it.

options.text: It does not abstract, since an outline is a record of what was actually observed.
options.misconception: confuses accurate observation with non-abstraction

options.text: It abstracts because the marsh has no interior detail, so nothing could have been included.
options.misconception: attributes the simplification to the subject's nature

options.text: It abstracts by selecting one feature, so the subject becomes the relation that feature reveals.
It does not abstract, because abstraction must exclude the recognisable entirely.
options.misconception: sets a stricter definition than the term requires

questions.explanation: Abstraction lies in the selection that turns a subject into chosen relations, and an outline is such a selection. Absence of detail, accurate observation and a ban on recognisable form miss that decision.

options.misconception: reduces the arrangement to a conservation precaution

questions.explanation: Flat colour fields and a refusal of objects direct attention to colour relations, so colour becomes the subject rather than a description. Skill, conservation and spatial effect do not explain why they matter.

questions.explanation: A steady change across a performance shows the event developing in time, which is part of what makes it a work rather than a fixed image. Fixity and acoustic explanations do not fit the record.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A work that is a set of instructions
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a set of instructions is in relation to its work
questions.stem: Writing up the method for a patchwork assembled from written steps, you must explain what the instructions are to the work.

answer.exemplar: The instructions are the work itself, not a description of it. They set out a set of conditions, materials and operations, and they exist as a stable object whether or not anyone ever carries them out. Each realisation that follows is a performance of those conditions rather than the work, which is why the sheet can be printed, copied and handed on while remaining the single, unchanging thing that was made.

questions.explanation: An instruction-based work is the specification, which persists unchanged while realisations come and go. That makes the sheet the work and each performance one of its instances, not the reverse.
questions.hint: Ask which object remains constant.

questions.topic: The readymade and the question of authorship
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish performing a work from designating a found object

stimulus.body: A granite kerbstone, chipped along one edge, is displayed alone on a low plinth with a label giving its location, the year it was lifted and the date it was set down. The label notes that the stone was not cut, worked or altered in any way.

questions.stem: A curator asks how a performance differs from a work whose maker changed nothing about the object at all.

options.text: Neither is a work, since art requires a visible alteration to the object involved.
options.misconception: requires material alteration for artistic status

options.text: Both are works, since any act of attention can be presented as art.
options.misconception: collapses distinct kinds of work into any attentive act

options.text: Performing sets conditions in time, while displaying asserts authorship through the act of choice.
The display is the work only if the stone is moved to a better position later on.
options.misconception: ties authorship to a later adjustment of placement

questions.explanation: Performing sets conditions in time and leaves a trace in memory and records, while designating a found object claims authorship through selection and placement. Attention, material alteration and later repositioning do not separate the two cases.
questions.hint: Ask what each case does rather than what it shows.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What colour field scale does to looking
questions.learningObjective: Describe the shift in looking produced by a room-filling colour
questions.stem: Explaining to a funder what an installation of colour does to the people standing in it, you must describe the shift in looking.

answer.exemplar: When colour covers a large area, the viewer stops reading the wall as a surface with things on it and begins to read it as an area, an edge, a relation. Because the field gives nothing to identify, the eye turns outward to the size of the room, to the body of the person standing there, and to the boundary where the colour stops. The picture is therefore inseparable from the architecture it fills, which is why the dimensions of the site decide what the work is.

questions.explanation: A large colour field shifts looking from depicted things to areas, edges and the viewer's body, which is why the room's size enters the work. Detail, hue alone and framing do not explain the change.
questions.hint: Ask where the viewer looks when nothing is depicted.

options.misconception: substitutes the plan of the project for the performed work

options.text: The work cannot exist, since without documentation there is nothing to collect or preserve.
options.misconception: assumes art requires a surviving document

options.misconception: redirects the subject from the action to the landscape

options.text: The work is the repeated act itself, so it exists in the doing rather than in any surviving record.

questions.explanation: A work performed and never recorded exists in the doing, with repetition marking it as a work rather than an accident. Documentation, the landscape and the long project each describe something else.

questions.topic: Abstraction as a decision about subject
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an abstraction is not a failed copy
questions.stem: Explaining to a class why an abstraction is not a failed copy, you must set out the decision it records.

answer.exemplar: An abstraction is not a copy that went wrong; it is a made choice about what a subject is. The maker selects certain features, scales, colours or relations and leaves the rest aside, and those selections are presented so that they can be seen as a subject with its own logic. Nothing has failed in the process, because the work's aim was never to reproduce the appearance of a thing. What the viewer is asked to read is the arrangement the maker chose.

questions.explanation: Abstraction is a made decision about what counts as the subject, so nothing in it has failed. Treating it as a defective copy mistakes a chosen arrangement for an unsuccessful likeness.
questions.hint: Ask whether the work was aiming at a likeness.

Collage works through confusion, since disagreement proves that meaning is constructed by viewers.
options.misconception: treats observer disagreement as proof of a designed effect

options.text: Collage elements must be anonymous, since a fragment cannot be identified once it is cut.
options.misconception: infers anonymity from the act of cutting

questions.explanation: Seven of ten features described alike suggests fragments are legible as distinct elements, the condition for a shared account. Unreadability, deliberate confusion and anonymity miss what the agreement indicates.
questions.hint: Ask what high agreement lets you say.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What collage does to drawing and making
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the operation of a readymade from that of a collage
questions.stem: Explaining to a technician why a readymade is not the same as a collage, you must distinguish the two operations.

answer.exemplar: The readymade keeps the found object intact and claims authorship through the decision to select and place it. The collage cuts, tears and rearranges, so the material is altered and its relationships are authored in the making. One shifts attention to the act of designation; the other to the act of composition. Treating them alike mistakes the presence of a found thing for the presence of a made one.

questions.explanation: A readymade claims authorship through selection, while a collage authors relationships through cutting and composition. Confusing the two mistakes a found thing for a made one.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the material in each case.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What colour field scale does to looking
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the filled proportion of a grid used to map colour areas
questions.stem: A playback unit records a sound every thirty seconds, and you are counting the cells of a twenty by twenty grid in which 84 cells were left blank. What percentage of the grid is filled?
questions.explanation: The grid holds 400 cells and 84 are blank, so 316 are filled, which is 79 per cent. The proportion stands for how much of a picture a single colour field occupies.
questions.hint: Fill the grid, then divide by the whole.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why an installation depends on its site
questions.learningObjective: Explain how relocation altered a site-dependent display

stimulus.body: A display of sounds recorded on the marsh was installed in a disused pumping station 30 kilometres away, and visitors there reported hearing nothing but machinery. The curator's note records that the works were re-recorded to include local sounds and reinstalled in the original building the following spring.

questions.stem: Reviewing a log of images collected during the survey, you find a display of field recordings installed far from the marsh and later reworked in place.

options.text: The original display failed technically, since machinery noise is a fault in the recording.
options.misconception: attributes the difference to a technical fault

options.text: The curator improved the work, since the recordings were simply better in their new setting.
options.misconception: explains a change of work as an improvement in quality

options.text: The site supplied material the work depended on, so its removal altered what the display became.
The display was portable, so the same work was simply moved to a better building.
options.misconception: assumes portability rules out dependence on a site

questions.explanation: The different experience in the pumping station shows surroundings entered the work, and re-recording for the original site confirms that dependence. Improvement, fault and portability each describe it wrongly.
questions.hint: Ask what the new building did to the recording.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A work that is a set of instructions
questions.learningObjective: Separate the score from the performance it produces
questions.stem: Comparing two accounts of what makes a work, you must separate the score from the performance it produces.

options.text: The score is the work only when no performance follows, since performance ends the work.
options.misconception: makes the work depend on the absence of performance

options.text: The score is a plan and the performance is the work, since only the event exists for others.
options.misconception: assigns the work's identity to the event alone

options.text: The score and the performance are equally the work, since each is made by a different person.
options.misconception: splits the work evenly between plan and realisation

options.text: The score is the work and the performance is one realisation, since the score persists unchanged.

questions.explanation: An instruction-based work is the specification, and each performance is one realisation, so the score persists while performances vary. A plan, an equal split and a work ending with performance misplace the relation.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two remains unchanged.
